newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentines, Indonesians haggle over shoes and beef.
newsitem.headline: Argentines, Indonesians haggle over shoes and beef.

text.p: Indonesia's Industry and Trade Minister Tunky Ariwibowo told Argentine officials here Thursday he wants lower tariffs on shoes, but Indonesia is in no hurry to open its 200-million strong market to Argentine beef.
Ariwibowo, leading a trade mission to South America, met President Carlos Menem and presented Indonesia's call for lower shoe tariffs.
"It's not only affecting Indonesia but affecting all the countries that export shoes and other products into this country," the minister told reporters later Thursday.
But the Argentines have yet to make concessions.
"We are still in the process of discussing it," he said.

Asked whether Indonesia was about to open up its large and fast-growing market to Argentine beef, Ariwibowo said that the South Americans' request was being considered and changed the subject to his country's trade gap.

He said, "The export import figures over the past few years have always produced a surplus for Argentina. In 1995, Indonesia exported to Argentina about $47 million. We imported from Argentina more than $220 million."
He noted that Argentine exports to Indonesia more than doubled in 1995, while Indonesian exports to Argentina expanded by only six percent.

Asked whether Indonesia was waiting for any Argentine gesture before relaxing beef import rules, the minister replied, "Not as such. But of course we would like to see trade more balanced between Argentina and Indonesia."
Asia's increasing appetite for meat is Argentina's great hope for boosting its beef exports, which were for decades restricted by problems with foot and mouth disease.
The Indonesian delegation, which includes 35 businessmen, is also looking for business opportunities in areas including aircraft manufacture and telecommunications.

Indonesia Chamber of Commerce and Industry president Aburizal Bakrie said that ARTS International, part of his personal business group, was negotiating to sell and eventually produce rural telephone systems in Argentina.
Another Bakrie firm was examining a possible $300 million joint-venture with Argentine steel maker Siderca to produce stainless steel tubes in Indonesia.

Bakrie said he hoped ASEAN member countries will use Argentina as a base to penetrate the Mercosur customs union, which also groups Brazil, Uruguay and Paraguay, and that Mercosur will launch its ASEAN drive through Indonesia.
The Indonesian mission follows a visit by Menem to Indonesia and Malaysia in August.
The mission will leave Argentina for Sao Paulo on Sunday, and from Brazil for Mexico on Tuesday.
